listing_view.reasoning: Demand is strong: the book went from under 1x on day two's afternoon to ~31x by close on day three [subscription history in verified figures], which typically means heavy last-day retail/QIB momentum on a small ₹631m issue and a likely listing pop. My concern is that this demand is momentum-driven on a tiny float while the underlying numbers are deteriorating — so the pop says nothing about value. Score is high on demand evidence alone, not on fundamentals.

longterm_view.reasoning: The business is shrinking at both ends: revenue and PAT are down over two years, and ROCE/ROE have collapsed from ~20%/15% to 10.6%/7.6% [business, page 437]. Worse, reported profit is not arriving as cash — operating cash flow was negative two of three years (latest: −₹1,970m on ₹1,320m PAT) while receivable days blew out from 35 to 137, meaning earnings quality is poor and the customer base is paying much slower. Margins are still fat (30%+ EBITDA), which is the one thing stopping a lower score, but fat margins with negative cash conversion is the classic profile of profits that exist mainly on paper.

governance.reasoning: SEBI imposed a penalty on the Company [litigation, page 608], there is an open SEBI show-cause notice [litigation, page 608], and the Company as a registered Investment Adviser received a separate SCN [litigation, page 610] — multiple regulatory touchpoints, each individually small, but a pattern. The prospectus also discloses promoter pledging/collateral of bank guarantees [promoters, page 533]. Nothing here is disqualifying, but for a financial-services issuer the regulator's attention is a real flag.

key_risks.why_it_matters: Latest-year operating cash flow is −₹1,970m against ₹1,320m PAT, so the earnings the IPO is priced on have not materialised as cash.
Customers now take 137 days to pay versus 35 two years ago; either revenue is being booked ahead of collection or the customer base has weakened — both impair the balance sheet.
ROCE fell from 20.4% to 10.6% and ROE to 7.6%, so incremental rupees are earning less — the opposite of what a growth-priced IPO needs.
A paid penalty plus an open show-cause notice against a SEBI-registered adviser raises the risk of future restrictions on the core licensed activity.
₹1,836.50 lakh of assets kept as collateral for bank guarantees signals contingent obligations sitting against the company.

answers.question: where did the money go — receivables, inventory, or both?
answers.answer: Receivables, demonstrably: collection period stretched from 35 to 137 days over two years, and operating cash flow swung from +₹11,019m to −₹3,186m to −₹1,970m, consistent with cash being trapped in unpaid customer balances rather than profit. I cannot confirm or exclude an inventory build — no inventory line was given to me — so 'both' is possible but unproven; what is proven is that receivables alone are large enough to explain the cash drain.

answers.question: who are the customers, and is any of it disputed?
answers.answer: The extracts never name a single customer, concentration, or customer dispute — the only disputes disclosed are regulatory: a SEBI penalty paid by the Company and an open SEBI show-cause notice, including one against the Company in its capacity as a registered Investment Adviser. So: customers unknown; the disclosed disputes are with the regulator, not customers, and given receivables at 137 days the absence of any customer-level disclosure is itself a gap.

answer.what_would_change_my_mind: Evidence that the receivables spike is a one-off timing effect already reversing (e.g., post-year-end collections) and that operating cash flow normalised would move my long-term view up meaningfully. Conversely, the fresh-issue/OFS split and any basis-for-price chapter — neither of which I was given — could sharpen the view in either direction; if this is largely an offer for sale by promoters into a shrinking, cash-negative business, my long-term score goes lower.
